Okay. We're on reel number two with Wallace Davenport in November the 14th, 1995. Tell me the story about your mother and the horn. How'd you get your first horn?

Well, at the school, McDonald's 36, the kids who wanted to play music, they had to put up a dollar a week. And most of the dollar was for the horn. And after 50 lessons, the horn is yours. So the horn didn't cost for $50. No, it didn't cost $50. It cost $20. It cost $25. So, and yeah, when she said she was going to turn the horn in because she couldn't pay for any more lessons. And I cried so much until she went and got on a knee and started praying. She was the type of woman that believed in her. She believed in prayers. And she prayed and asked the Lord to let her give me some more lessons, pay for some more lessons. And something happened. She got another little job. See, because the job she had, she wasn't making but a dollar a week. And my father, well, he was a jack of all trades. He used to do things for people in the neighborhood and they would pay him. Like, at the time, like when you go to a grocery store and buy chicken or turkey, they didn't have any frozen chicken and turkey. You had to buy them alive and take him home and kill him. Well, a lot of those men in the neighborhood, a lot of women, they didn't know how to kill a chicken. So they would get my dad and give him fifty cents to kill the chicken. And he would save that money up and that kind of helped to pay for our music lessons. And he did a lot of things making extra money. But the extra money he made wasn't much. He might fix your clock for ten cents, a nickel. There wasn't much money around then. And like when we'd go to church, we used to put a penny in the collection. And something old. When they passed the flag. Yeah, we put a penny. But at that time,
a penny was a lot of money. Well, what was the times of the year of the celebrations? What was Christmas like for your family? Oh, yeah. We had a big Christmas.

We had a big Christmas dinner. We had a Christmas tree. Then we had a lot of toys. And before I started playing trumpet, I always remembered on Christmas I would get a trumpet, a toy trumpet. This was before you really had a real trumpet? Yeah, just before I started school. When I think back about when I was two and three years old, I always had a trumpet. You didn't blow it the way you blow it, you just hum it. Do-do-do-do-do-do-do-do-do-do.
Sort of like a kazoov. Yeah, kazoov. Yeah. So how many, would the whole family be there?

I mean you had relatives came over for Christmas? No, no, no, no, no, no. Just the five of us. My father, my mother, my sister, my cousin, and me. What was your cousin's name again? Margie. Margie what? At that time, Margie Dickerson. Oh, okay. So she was from your mother's, your

mother's side. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Anyway, I have a lot more to ask you. Were there any saloons in your neighborhood? You said you played at different places, but would you play at places in your neighborhood?

No, no. There were saloons in the neighborhood, but they didn't have any music. Now, there was music downtown, and some of the places uptown, like the Pigpen. Did you go to the Pigpen? Oh, I went there once. Now those are the players who played, like the Pigpen and some of those old places, Louis Armstrong played there. See, a lot of people think that Louis Armstrong played on Bourbon Street. Because people come in and ask me, they say, oh, did Louis Armstrong play here? No. And when he played at Preservation Heart, I said, no, he didn't play on Bourbon Street at all. There wasn't no Bourbon. Bourbon Street didn't have entertainment at that time. Yeah. But they think that Louis Armstrong played in the French Quarter. And when Louis Armstrong learned how to play well enough to make some money, he left and went to Chicago. King Oliver was sitting for him to come to Chicago, Joe Oliver. And he stayed in Chicago until he moved to New York. When he left Chicago, he left King Oliver Band and went to New York to play
with Fletcher Henderson. Well, you mentioned the Pigpen. Did you ever, that was on Decatur Street?
No, the Pigpen was on Liberty and Phillip. Liberty and Phillip. Okay.
Uptown, Uptown Street. All right. This, what year is this?

Now, this, in around 1933, 32, 33, is when I went there. But, uh. What kind of place was it? Just a dance hall? It wasn't anything polished. It was just like a dive. But that was the only place that we had to go to have entertainment. I mean, if you didn't go to one of those places, you'd go to a house where they used to have those fish fries. Like, did you ever hear that number, Saturday night, fish fries? Sure. Sure, Louie Jugg. Well, who was playing at the
Pigpen? Did you play at the Pigpen? I played there once, with Professor Victor's band. But

that's where the old, I mean, that's where the professional musicians played. Now what I mean by professional musicians, the guys who were playing for the big money, a dollar and a half a night. Right. Were these dances they played for? Yeah, dances, yeah. Dances. Sometimes I think about the money that they paid us, and the money that the musicians were, and they were glad to make that money. Some of them used to play for nothing. There are some places where the guys used to go and play for drinks. Sure. They played for drinks. Did you hear a lot of piano players? Oh yeah. And just about every neighborhood you go and go into uptown, you'll hear a piano. If you didn't hear a piano, you would hear a record, Bessie Smith Lewis, all the wrong with King Oliver. In the saloon played? Well I thought, no, no, I'm talking about like when you're walking down the street.
Oh, when you're walking down the street. You're going to hear this. You would hear either records or pianos coming from people's houses. And what would they be

playing on the piano? The blues. They played blues. And that's all you would hear, the blues. Like what numbers, when you say? They would make up the blues. They would make up the blues. They used the blues pattern and just improvised. They didn't know what they were doing. They didn't know they were improvising. They just
started playing. So they started playing. So a lot of families that had pianos, I mean people played blues. Was there a lot of blues played in the saloons?

Yeah. That's all they would play in the saloons, was blues. Were they just solo pianists? Yeah. Most of the piano players who were really popular, they played piano and sang too. They would sing and play the piano. And there's a guy who, did you ever hear of Trits Washington? Sure. Yeah. He was the first one to take, he took me on my first big job. So what took you on your first big job? Yeah, at the Cotton Club. Yeah, just built a new place, they had rebuilt a place on Rampart Street where he had gambling and drinking. And it was really a nice place, you know. And he came to my house nice, my mother, because I played there with a lot of people. At that time I was about, I couldn't have been no more than 14. What was the Cotton Club like? It was, well see, there was a Cotton Club there, but you remodel it. Remodel it. When you remodel it, it was, I think they got that name from the Cotton Club in New York. Because I'm more than sure New York had a Cotton Club before in New Orleans. Yeah. Then they had another club, called a Tick Tock. There was a club and they had dancing there too. That was on Rampart Street. Did you work at that club? I never worked there. Although Victor, the band played there, but I had gotten out of the band. I got out of the band before I played at the Tick Tock. Now the senior band would play there a lot. And after I got out of the band, then the senior band started traveling around Louisiana, so they put the junior band in there, the Tick Tock. And the rhythm club,
that was the top place. The rhythm club was the top place?

Yeah. The rhythm club was where all the top bands would come, you know, like Count Basie and Lionel Hampton and Andy Kirk, the Sunset Royal. But that was a good band out of Florida. For those bands you used to play at the Tick Tock. Did you go to the rhythm club? Oh yeah. That was the first time I heard Louis Armstrong was at the rhythm club. Louis Armstrong came and I had to play one Sunday. And I had to hurry and buy my advance ticket. Because if you wait until that night and pay it to do it, it was a dollar. But if you buy your advance ticket, it was 90 cents. Yeah, advance ticket was 90 cents. That's all you had to pay to hear those great guys.
She wanted to save that money.
Yeah, save 10 cents.
What do you remember about that night when you saw Louis?
I didn't dance, I had my girlfriend with me. And I didn't dance at all, it was a dance. I just stood up in front of the bandstand just looking at him, just looking at him playing the trumpet.
Did you try to watch his fingering?

No. But you know that watching the fingering, that's something those old musicians used to fear. And the thing that they would do, to me nothing didn't make sense. They would take a handkerchief and put it over their fingers so the other trumpet player wouldn't see it. But if a guy got any kind of musical, yeah, you don't have to.
He don't have to.
Because like if you learn a tune from the record, nobody ever put a package over the tape or the record.
Right. Anything else you remember about Louis at the Rhythm Club, or the Rhythm Club in general?

Well, I went there one time and heard the Six Brown Cats. You ever hear them? Yeah. It was Thomas Jefferson, Adam Lambert, and Famous Lambert, and Stanley Williams. That was a good band. They had a good band. They played at the Rhythm Club every Sunday in the afternoon.
Was it always a place where you, was it a sit down place or could you dance?

Yeah, dance, you could sit down. There was a table, you can get a table. You get a table and there's a dancing area. Did you know who ran the club? Who was the club owner? Yeah, a guy, a TikTok guy named Beansie. Oh, Beansie Fournier?
Yeah.

Okay. Then the Rhythm Club, uh, uh. I think Beansie was at the TikTok. Yeah, TikTok. And the guy at the Rhythm Club, oh, I've forgotten his name. Oh, I've forgotten his name. Now at the Elks, that was a club, the Elks Club. They had the, the night club they had there with Elks. They were run by a club, a group of fellas.
To any of the places you remember going? I mean to listen to music? Rather, you know, in the audience rather than as a player?

Yeah, now the WPA band, that's the band they had, where my first teacher was teaching, because when he started directing the WPA band, he had to give up his students. He couldn't have any other job, couldn't have another job working with the WPA band. But he, when he was there with the WPA band, I used to go out in Shakespeare Park. They call it Davis Park now. And I would go out there and hear them play, because there was a trumpet player in that band. I used to admire his tone, his style. A fellow named Gilbert Young, he had a lot of influence over me. His playing influenced me a lot. He had a big pretty tone, a big pretty sound. And there were so many trumpet players that I heard that were playing on the trucks. I didn't get a chance to hear them, just saw them once. Now, they didn't have any sound trucks to go around to advertise. Like if you want to advertise something, you get a band and they get a truck and they play on the truck. Now like that's where this, where tailgate comes from. See like they would put a tailgate down on the truck and have the trombone play out there. See because if you put the trombone play in the back, he'd be jiggled everybody with the slide. Now I used to play on the truck. I used to play on the truck. I used to play on the truck. I was a little boy. And I remember the best jobs musicians could have at that time was doing mardi gras. Yeah, tell me about mardi gras. Now mardi gras. We get a job. All the while we've been playing for a dollar and a half, a dollar. Five dollars at the most. But when you play on mardi gras at the most. Who'd you work for on Mardi Gras Day?

Oh, that's been so long, I forgot. Different clubs, the clubs, like you have a pleasure club, about 10 people, when you rent a truck, and they have the band on there, on the truck, and they have a lot of whiskey, they have a good time, and with the music on there, they're dancing on the truck.

No, they have a regular route.
A regular route.

You know one time I played a carnival parade, and we were supposed to follow Rex. Yeah. And the guy, the president of the club, it was a white club too, and they gave us a fifth of whiskey. So I was standing next, I was marching with a guy named Son Johnson, have you heard of Son Johnson? Yeah. He was on this side of me, and I remember playing the horn, take me a drink, play the horn, give him the, because he couldn't carry the whiskey and play his horn too, because you have to have two hands to play the saxophone. So we messed around and drinking all that liquor, and we got drunk in the parade. And the band made a turn, and we kept straight. We kept going straight. And then we heard people behind us clapping, and we didn't hear any drums, we didn't hear another horn. So when we looked around, we didn't know where the band turned.
Yeah.
We just kept going. The whole Rex parade went one way, and we were going another way, just Son Johnson and me.

I think still, people still do that today. I think I've been to a few parades. Yeah. People still do that. What'd you do, what'd you do as a kid on Mardi Gras Day? Was that a special day for you, for your family?

Yes and no. Well, before I would, before I started playing in the parades, and playing on the trucks, we'd stay in front of our house, either go to a jack, two blocks away from our home, where they had the funeral home. That's where the King Zulu used to go and drink his toast. Well, we would go there and see them. Then we would go to Canal, I mean to St. Charles and Frays, and see Rex. Then we'd come on back home, and just stay in front of our house. There wasn't too much going on out there. Because Mardi Gras used to be dangerous. Well, it's still dangerous. And see, like the Indians, those guys would fight when they meet up. See, like this tribe from downtown, meet the tribe from uptown, and they would fight and shoot each other, cut up each other. Some of them would carry hatchets. But now they don't do that anymore. And they'd be friends. They'd be like he belonged to one tribe, and I belonged to another tribe. All during the year, we'd go out and drink. The Mardi Gras day come, we'd start drinking. Then I'm going to bring up something that you did to make me angry. And then we'd start fighting and shooting.
Were you scared of the Indians as a child?
Yeah. As long as I didn't see, as long as I was watching one tribe, I would watch. But if I see another tribe two blocks away, I'd make it home.
Because you knew there was going to be a battle.

Now, sometimes they would meet and there wasn't a battle. One of the chiefs would tell the other one, they would sit and say, you have your guys on this side and I have my guys on this side. And I'd tell you, Oomba! That means get down on your knees. And the guy, if he Oomba, well, they'll laugh at him and make jokes out that he's supposed to be a coward. They wouldn't do anything. But if he said, Oomba! The guy said, D'Oomba! I don't know how! Then he start fighting. And the next day, you see all these Indians coming out of jail with the costumes on. But they have changed now. What they try to do now is try to out-dress each other. That's how they fight now. Pretty much so.
Do you remember names of any of the tribes that you saw?
Yeah, the yellow Pocahontas, the Creole Wild West. And, well, it was the most popular. It was the most popular.
So this was up in your neighborhood as a kid. Where were you living then?
On first, between Franklin and Liberty.
On first, between Franklin and Liberty. Did you know any of the Indians personally? Did you know any of the people? Did you know anybody who joined a tribe? Yeah, there was a guy.
One of the tribes? Yeah. Yeah. But I was, I didn't, see at that time, the Indians were supposed to be the lowest type of people
in the parade.

People used to like to watch them because they were dressed. Now some people who liked to watch fights, they would go out there and watch a fight until they start shooting. When they start shooting, then everybody's rotten.
But if you told your mother, I'm going to join the Indians, I'm going to join one of the tribes?

Oh, no, no. I wouldn't even mention it. They would have been upset? Yes, indeed. They never would have let me have gone out there with the men. Now when I was about four and five years old, every Mardi Grotti would buy me a cowboy outfit. They had my little pistol there and I had one of my cowboy outfit.

Yeah. But I wouldn't go out by myself. My mother would be with me. She wouldn't let us out of our sight on Mardi Grotti. Then we divorced. Both of us got married again. But we were the best of friends and we still go to the same church. We'd sit down and laugh and joke about the things we used to do. We used to cheat on each other. We were the best of friends. And Buffer would say if we hadn't known then, like we know now, we would joke right together. See, I had the wrong idea about marriage. I thought when you marry a woman that was your property, your owner. Well a lot of people, that's the way it was a long time ago. But like now, these women, they want to do their thing. So Gene wasn't like that? She wanted to have her own life?

Yeah. You see, I was married and I had my family to take care of.

Now, were there times when you had, when you all played, say for a white audience? Mm-hmm. Where, where, there were white women? Mm-hmm. Was that a problem?

And you try, oh, you try to be nice, yeah, yeah, well, yeah, well, look, come on, come here, come here, and man, they'd throw their arms around you and hug you. So this woman wrote Lee a note and gave it to the white bartender to pass it over to Lee. And, and so, sometimes something happened that, that they... No, no.
See, a lot of guys would take chances. I didn't want to take, I didn't want to take any chances. Because I have too many, I had too many other women. Mm-hmm.
Sure. So the only things that would happen is you'd get past the note, you wouldn't, but you wouldn't follow through on it.
Now, you know like, there, I know you've heard the expression, Uncle Tom. Sure. And I tell people I've only known Uncle Tom once in my life.
Explain what you mean by Uncle Tom, because I've, I've heard, you know, I've heard the expression. Yeah, Uncle Tom.
